## TL;DR

Added shared plain-language classification for common agent CLI failures and applied it to failed-run escalation and engineer crash recovery. Added table-driven classifier coverage and a short user-facing note. The classifier recognizes authentication failures, unavailable models (including Cursor's “Cannot use this model” wording), Copilot Auto-tier catalog failures, usage limits, and common network errors. Unknown failures pass through unchanged. Known failures retain their source text inline as a CLI detail.

## Work and rationale

The existing failure path already records a useful per-task detail when an agent exits unsuccessfully. That detail is stored in the task's needs-input fields, which are rendered by the task card and drawer. The missing piece was consistent interpretation: Copilot had a specialized enrichment helper, while auth, model, and network failures from other CLIs were left as raw output. I introduced a core classifier so the mapping is shared and can be tested without invoking a CLI or contacting a service.

The classifier returns a reason identifier, a short explanation, and a next step. It deliberately handles Copilot's Auto-tier messages before the generic model matcher because those messages describe a catalog mismatch rather than a general transport or billing error. Cursor's “Cannot use this model: composer-2.5” message extracts the model identifier for a useful sentence. If the input does not match a known class, the function returns null and the existing raw-tail behavior remains available.

Failure escalation now formats known messages before placing them in the task's needs-input detail. The raw CLI text is retained in a parenthetical CLI field, so the short explanation does not erase diagnostic evidence. The task card and drawer consume the same needs-input detail, so this applies to the existing task-level surfaces without creating a second transient state system.

The shared attention event store already supports durable, stable-key notices. I added one current agent-failure event per CLI for auth and unavailable-model failures, using a stable CLI key so failures across multiple tasks replace the same notice. A clean later run clears that CLI's notice. The notice is intentionally limited to actionable auth/model setup errors; ordinary transient network failures and time-based usage limits do not create a persistent board-level setup notice.

Crash recovery now classifies the prior failure before composing the relaunch prompt and activity note. That gives the next agent a reason in plain language and includes the CLI's raw failure detail. The existing recovery activity remains attached to the task, where the board's task activity and attention links can lead the user to the relevant context.

## Approaches tried

I followed the existing Copilot failure-enrichment pattern and extracted the cross-CLI mapping into a core module rather than expanding the Copilot-specific helper. I reused task needs-input details for task surfaces and the durable attention event store for board notices. No new dependency or configuration setting was introduced.

Tests use fixed sample strings only. They do not spawn a provider CLI, make network requests, or depend on account credentials. The table covers Cursor model rejection, Claude expired OAuth, the Copilot Auto-tier failure, usage limits, and DNS/network failure, plus unknown-text passthrough and retention of the raw detail.

## Challenges and blockers

The server already had multiple failure paths: one-shot enrichment, engineer exit escalation, reviewer completion, and engineer crash recovery. This change generalizes the shared engineer failure summary and the explicit crash-recovery reason while preserving the existing Copilot enrichment. Provider usage-limit detection is also already connected to budget management; the new classifier avoids changing that policy and only provides human-readable failure copy.

The main validation issue was API-route parity: the new Agents-page last-run endpoint is UI-only, so the parity test required an explicit entry in the existing UI-only route allowlist. I added that narrow exemption. The scoped check then passed remotely on the retry host after the first runner hung, including build, 302 changed-path test files, browser smoke, contrast audit, formatting, and lint. Local guards also passed, including the user-docs build.

## Key learnings

Agent CLI errors are most useful when treated as structured categories with both a human sentence and the untouched source text. A core pure function makes that mapping cheap to exercise and safe to reuse across runtime contexts. Stable notice identity is also essential: it turns repeated failures across tasks into one board-level item, while a successful run can clear it deterministically. The pure classifier, notice lifecycle tests, and existing local test fakes kept these checks independent of networks and real provider accounts.
